title: Recent advances in the assembly of high-nuclearity lanthanide clusters
claim: Small anions are needed to grow higher-nuclearity lanthanide clusters, and slow release of anions, multiple anions, or mixed anions templates assembly more effectively than a single anion because they disperse concentrated positive charge while also balancing charge.
explanation: Metal–metal repulsion is presented as the barrier to increasing nuclearity. Halides first showed that a simple anion can template clusters (illustrated by I−-templated Dy26), but the review argues that slowly generated anions and several anions in different coordination modes both induce the framework and stabilize it. Carbonate is highlighted as a template that can come from in situ ligand decomposition or atmospheric CO2.
scope: High-nuclearity lanthanide hydroxide clusters using halide or oxoanion templates.
conditions: Slow release is achieved by in situ ligand or solvent decomposition, often under hydro/solvothermal conditions, or by absorption of atmospheric CO2 at a suitable pH.
caveats: The advantage over a single-anion template is a comparative claim based on the surveyed clusters (Table 1), not a quantitative ranking of template strength.
